pieces.title: Missing for six years, found by a reporter: David Livingstone
pieces.hook: He treated fame as a tool for something larger. He said the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people…
pieces.takeaway: He treated fame as a tool for something larger. He said the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people”—and he wanted that weight for the fight against the slave trade.
pieces.imageCredit: Thomas Annan · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: David Livingstone (1813–1873) was a Scottish doctor, missionary, and explorer. On this day 155 years ago—10 November 1871—the American journalist Stanley found him at Ujiji, beside Lake Tanganyika in what is now Tanzania. The greeting is said to have begun, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?

paras.lead: Into the spinning mill at ten
parts: He was born on 19 March 1813 in a cotton-mill tenement at Blantyre, Scotland, the second of seven children. At ten he went into the mill as a piecer, working from 6 in the morning until 8 at night, and after work he still went to the village school.

He read a pamphlet urging that “a missionary should study medicine first,” and he meant to practice and preach in China. With the First Opium War about to begin, the London Missionary Society did not send him. In November 1840 he qualified as a doctor in Glasgow and was ordained; he sailed that same month and reached southern Africa in March 1841.

paras.lead: A lion crushed his left arm
parts: In February 1844, at Mabotsa in what is now Botswana, he shot at a lion that was attacking the flocks. As he reloaded, the lion sprang and crushed his left arm. Mebalwe, an African church deacon, fired and drew the lion off, and that saved him. He could never raise that arm above his shoulder again.
In January 1845 he married Mary Moffat, who had nursed him.

He was later called “Africa’s greatest missionary,” yet the record shows only one formal convert: Sechele, chief of the Kwena. Sechele kept the rainmaking rite. Neil Parsons of the University of Botswana argues that Sechele’s part in spreading Christianity through nineteenth-century southern Africa was almost greater than that of any European missionary.

From 1852 to 1856, with guides and porters sent by the Kololo chief Sekeletu (27 at first, later 114), he walked west from the middle Zambezi to Luanda on the Atlantic, then back and east to Quelimane on the Indian Ocean. On 16 November 1855 he became the first European on record to see the falls local people called “the smoke that thunders,” and he named them Victoria Falls after the queen.

paras.lead: A celebrity, and a new employer
parts: He was back in Britain at the end of 1856. The next year Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa became a bestseller. The London Missionary Society said it could not readily fund a trade-route expedition “so remote from preaching the gospel,” so in 1857 he resigned, returned to Africa as a British consul, and took £5,000 from the government.

The Zambezi expedition of 1858–1864 went badly. The Kebrabasa rapids blocked the river; the steamer could not pass. His wife Mary died of malaria in April 1862. John Kirk, the expedition’s doctor, wrote that he was “a most unsafe leader.” In 1864 the government recalled the party, and many newspapers called it a failure.

paras.lead: Looking for the source of the Nile
parts: In 1866 he set out from Zanzibar to find the source of the Nile. His medicines were stolen, and when he was very ill he could only travel with a slave traders’ caravan. On 15 July 1871, at the market of Nyangwe on the Lualaba, he watched Arab slave traders massacre about 400 Africans. The shock was severe, and he gave up going farther north.
For those years he was almost cut off. Of 44 letters he sent, only one reached Zanzibar.

paras.lead: A greeting that may have been composed later
parts: James Gordon Bennett of the New York Herald paid for the search. Stanley reached Zanzibar in March 1871, raised a party, walked about 1,100 kilometres, and found him at Ujiji on 10 November. The famous sentence is not in Stanley’s diary from the time—he tore out the relevant pages—and it is not in Livingstone’s own record either.

He did not go back with Stanley. On 1 May 1873 he died at Chitambo, in what is now Zambia, aged 60. His attendants Chuma and Susi buried his heart under a tree, then carried his body and his diary for 63 days and more than 1,600 kilometres to Bagamoyo on the coast. From there he was taken to Britain and buried in Westminster Abbey.

His books and diaries moved the British public against the East African slave trade. The slogan “Christianity, commerce, and civilization” was borrowed, in the decades after his death, by European colonial expansion. In the anti-colonial mood of the 1960s he was for a time “debunked.” Livingstone in Zambia, and Blantyre in Malawi, named for his home town, still keep those names.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Livingstone himself | View: Christianity plus “legitimate trade” could replace the slave trade. ; Interest: opening a Zambezi trade route, his own name, and funds. ; Worry: the slave trade keeps expanding. ; Basis: the slogan “Christianity, commerce, and civilization”; he told a friend the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people.”

The London Missionary Society | View: money should go to mission work, not to exploring trade routes. ; Interest: mission stations, and the safety of missionaries. ; Worry: the plan was drifting ever farther from preaching. ; Basis: a letter saying the directors could hardly fund a plan “so remote from preaching the gospel”; several members of the mission he sent to the Kololo died of malaria, and the biographer Tim Jeal argues that he overstated local conditions.

The British government and the Royal Geographical Society | View: it was worth paying to test Britain’s trade prospects on the Zambezi. ; Interest: commerce, geographical knowledge, and influence. ; Worry: the money would be wasted. ; Basis: a government grant of £5,000 and a consulship; the expedition was recalled in 1864; the Society gave him its gold medal.

African people on the ground | View: cooperation was possible, but on their own terms. ; Interest: trade routes, safety, and their own beliefs and customs. ; Worry: Boers and slave traders. ; Basis: Sekeletu sent people with him across the continent; Sechele kept rainmaking and polygamy; Chuma and Susi carried the body for 63 days.

Later judges | View: from “national hero,” to “a myth that has been taken apart,” to something more complicated. ; Interest: how colonial history is told. ; Worry: a personal hero story hides what colonization did. ; Basis: the scholar Alvyn Austin’s summary in 1997; 98th place in the 2002 BBC poll of the 100 greatest Britons; many African places still carry his name.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: He opposed the slave trade, yet late in life he depended on slave traders’ caravans for his life and his supplies. The ideal and the fact tied each other down.
The Missionary Society wanted “preaching.” The government wanted “a trade route.” He changed employers, and he also took the charge that he sacrificed the people around him for the cause.
Stanley and the New York Herald sold papers on “finding Livingstone,” and along the way they rebuilt a reputation that had already been slipping.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: He wanted “commerce” to replace the slave trade. In the decades after his death, the roads into the interior became the roads of European colonization. There is still no agreed judgment on the gap between the motive and the result.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?” is not in Stanley’s diary from the time. It may have been shaped afterward.
His estimate of deaths in the slave trade—“at most one in five lived to reach the market”—has been criticized as a serious exaggeration.
The detail of the Nyangwe massacre: spectral imaging of the original diary shows that the published text cut his doubts about his own attendants.

pieces.title: Forty thousand people queued for 13,000 pairs: ninety years of nylon
pieces.hook: On 4 January 1946 a queue formed outside a department store in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. People were there only…
pieces.imageCredit: Ed Westcott (U.S. Department of Energy) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 4 January 1946 a queue formed outside a department store in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. People were there only to buy a pair of nylon stockings. In those months, fights over stockings in several American cities became the “nylon riots.” In Pittsburgh, about 40,000 people queued for 13,000 pairs.

In 1927, on the advice of Charles Stine, director of its chemical department, DuPont set up small teams for “pioneering research” and brought Wallace Carothers, a lecturer at Harvard, to lead the work on polymers. At first he could stay with pure science.

In the spring of 1930 the team made two new polymers. One was neoprene, a synthetic rubber later used in quantity in the Second World War. The other was an elastic paste that became very tough when it cooled—the forerunner of nylon. After that the company told them to look for “a chemical combination suited to industrial use.”
On 28 February 1935 the first nylon, nylon 66, was synthesized. In 1938 Schlack at IG Farben made another: nylon 6.

paras.lead: He did not live to see the success
parts: Carothers had suffered from depression since he was young. In 1936 he became the first industrial organic chemist elected to the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, but he did not get better. He died in April 1937, sixteen months before nylon was shown to the public.

On 27 October 1938 DuPont announced nylon in New York: “the first man-made organic textile fiber,” made from “coal, water, and air,” “as strong as steel, as fine as a spider’s web.” Its first commercial use, though, was toothbrush bristles in 1938.
Later reports said nylon might be made from extracts of corpses. The panic made DuPont change the line and lead with “beautiful, and quick to dry.”

paras.lead: The first sale sold out in three hours
parts: On 24 October 1939 nylon stockings went on public sale for the first time in Wilmington, Delaware: 4,000 pairs were gone in three hours. On 15 May 1940 they went on sale nationwide, and 64 million pairs sold in the first year. They were not cheap. By weight they cost about 1.5 times silk ($4.27 a pound against $2.79).

DuPont later said the name was meant to be “No-Run,” but stockings do run, so that promise could not be made. The name was changed and changed again until it became nylon. The widespread story that it is New York (NY) plus London (Lon) is an urban legend.

From 11 February 1942 nylon was turned over to the military, for parachutes, tents, and rope. On the black market a pair of stockings sold for $20. Women without stockings drew a “seam” on their legs. From the end of the war until 1952, 80 percent of the world’s nylon went into stockings and underwear.

In China, nylon is called jinlun. In April 1958 the Jinzhou chemical plant made China’s first batch of caprolactam, and the Beijing fiber plant then spun it into filament. Because it was made in Jinzhou, the fiber was named jinlun.

paras.lead: Where it stands now: large, and under pressure
parts: Figures from the China Chemical Fibers Association: in 2025 China’s nylon output was 4.72 million tonnes, up 2.8 percent, and that growth was 3.5 percentage points slower than in 2024. The average operating rate was about 81 percent, down 8.64 percentage points. Longzhong Information counts domestic nylon 66 capacity in the first half of 2025 at about 1.271 million tonnes a year, up about 21 percent, with imports down by about a third.

Tough and long-lasting also means hard to break down. Discarded nylon fishing nets are one source of marine debris. Nylon is the fiber most used in American residential carpet, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimates that in 2018 only 9.2 percent of carpet was recycled and 73 percent went to landfill.
Companies such as Italy’s Aquafil recycle old nets into clothing fabric, but recycling costs more than new material, and the scale is still small.

blocks.title: A bottleneck that lasted decades: adiponitrile
blocks.text: Nylon 66 needs hexamethylenediamine, and the key raw material for that, adiponitrile, was long controlled by foreign firms such as Invista and Ascend. In 2021 China’s own adiponitrile capacity was only 100,000 tonnes, while consumption was 312,000 tonnes. On 1 August 2022 Qixiang Tengda announced that Tianchen Qixiang’s 200,000-tonne-a-year adiponitrile unit in Zibo, Shandong, had run the whole process and produced premium-grade product. It was the first industrial adiponitrile plant in China to use the butadiene route.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: DuPont | View: turn basic research into a large business. ; Interest: patents and market position. ; Worry: consumers would not trust an “artificial fiber.” ; Basis: a patent in September 1938, and a quick monopoly of the fiber; to answer the rumors, the advertising shifted to “coal, air, and water” and “beautiful, and quick to dry.”

Carothers and the researchers | View: get the science straight first. ; Interest: freedom to research, and academic recognition. ; Worry: being told to turn toward “what is useful.” ; Basis: after 1930 the team was told to look for a combination “suited to industrial use”; in 1936 he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences.

Consumers, especially women | View: stockings that look good, last, and can actually be bought. ; Interest: price and supply. ; Worry: runs, stuffiness, static. ; Basis: 64 million pairs in the first year; the “nylon riots” of 1945–1946; pure nylon does not absorb sweat and runs easily, so blends became more common.

The U.S. military and the wartime government | View: strategic materials come first. ; Interest: a steady supply of parachutes and rope. ; Worry: Japanese raw silk being cut off. ; Basis: from February 1942 nylon was turned over to the military; after the embargo on Japan, the United States could not import raw silk.

China’s nylon firms today | View: break the raw-material bottleneck, and differentiate. ; Interest: cost, operating rate, and profit. ; Worry: a price war in ordinary grades, and high inventories. ; Basis: domestic adiponitrile in 2022; an operating rate of about 81 percent in 2025, down 8.64 percentage points (China Chemical Fibers Association).

Environmental and recycling groups | View: durable also means hard to break down. ; Interest: less marine debris and less microplastic. ; Worry: recycling is too expensive and still too small. ; Basis: the EPA’s 9.2 percent carpet recycling rate for 2018; Patagonia’s investment in Bureo, which makes products from old nets; Aquafil recycling nets into fabric.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: DuPont wanted the selling point “as strong as steel,” and it also feared promising too much. It would not even use a name that said “no run.”
The war took stockings out of consumers’ hands. The “nylon riots” afterward showed, the other way around, how large the demand was.
Domestic adiponitrile broke the monopoly and lowered the cost. Expanding capacity then pushed ordinary grades into a price war.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The virtues of nylon—tough, durable, cheap—are exactly its environmental problem. The recycling technology exists, but it costs more than new material, and the market has not yet put a strong enough price on the difference.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The crowd figures for the “nylon riots” (40,000 people for 13,000 pairs) are estimates from reporting at the time.
Sources give two dates for Carothers’s death, 28 April and 29 April.
That jinlun was named for Jinzhou rests mainly on popular accounts from the industry association and from companies.

pieces.title: Revenue up 28 percent, the share price down 18 percent in a day: Axon’s third quarter
pieces.hook: After the U.S. market closed on 5 November, Axon, which makes Tasers and body cameras, reported its third quarter (through…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results after the close on 2026-11-05 (U.S. Eastern time); the close on 11-06 was down 18.18 percent
pieces.imageAlt: An officer wearing a body camera
pieces.imageCredit: Tony Webster · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: After the U.S. market closed on 5 November, Axon, which makes Tasers and body cameras, reported its third quarter (through 30 September): revenue of $909 million, up 28 percent, the company’s highest third quarter on record. The next day, 6 November, the share price closed down 18.18 percent, the largest one-day drop since 2013.

In 1993 the Smith brothers, Rick and Tom Smith, founded AIR TASER. With Jack Cover, a former NASA researcher who invented the stun gun, they changed the propellant from gunpowder to compressed nitrogen. The company listed in 2001, brought out its first body camera in 2008, and in April 2017 renamed itself Axon. Its headquarters are in Scottsdale, Arizona.

paras.lead: From selling the “gun” to selling the cloud
parts: It now has two parts: “connected devices” (Tasers, cameras, counter-drone equipment, and the like) and “software and services” (evidence cloud, AI report writing, 911 dispatch, and the like). This quarter software and services brought in $437 million, up 43 percent. Annual recurring revenue was $1.75 billion, up 40 percent. Net revenue retention from existing customers was 126 percent, which means those customers spent about a quarter more this year than last.

First, it missed expectations. Adjusted earnings were $1.72 a share; the LSEG analyst consensus cited by Reuters was $1.88. Revenue was also below the roughly $940 million expected. Second, it cut the full-year guide: revenue from $3.67–3.725 billion to $3.61–3.63 billion, and growth from 32–34 percent to about 30 percent, because three federal counter-drone deployments, about $130 million of revenue, were pushed out of this year.
Third, the fourth-quarter revenue guide of $990 million to $1.01 billion was below Wall Street’s roughly $1.06 billion.

The overall gross margin fell from 60.1 percent to 56.7 percent. The company’s explanation: a higher share of counter-drone equipment, more expensive memory chips, and new products still ramping. The gross margin on connected devices fell from 49.9 percent to 43.0 percent.

Operating cash flow this quarter was $20 million (against $60 million a year earlier), and free cash flow was an outflow of $19 million, mainly because the company spent about $100 million stocking inventory early against supply-chain risk. The full-year free-cash-flow guide was also cut, from about $450 million to $350–400 million.

paras.lead: The largest investment it has ever made
parts: The same day, Axon said it would invest another $1.2 billion, in cash and stock, in the drone company Skydio, taking its stake to about 37 percent and becoming Skydio’s exclusive distributor for public safety in the United States and Canada. Reuters reported a pre-money valuation of $5.2 billion for the deal.
The company called it “the largest single investment in Axon’s history.”

Axon is pushing “drone as first responder”: when a call comes in, send a drone before anyone else. Citing the company, Reuters said agencies using the setup cut response time on priority calls by as much as 65 percent, and that in about 80 percent of call-outs the drone arrived before the officer.

Needham kept a “buy,” but cut its target from $750 to $500, and warned that the company’s goal of “more than 30 percent growth in five-year orders” was at risk of being missed. Craig-Hallum cut the rating to “hold,” saying the Taser business was clearly short of expectations and that quarter-to-quarter swings could get larger.

The fact: revenue and orders are still growing, but growth is slower, the margin is thinner, cash has turned negative, and at the same time the company is spending $1.2 billion on a stake. The inference: for a company whose share price has long been set as “high growth,” the market often punishes not “no growth,” but “growth that has turned a corner.”

blocks.title: The orders are in fact still growing
blocks.text: “Future contracted bookings”—the part that is signed but not yet delivered—reached $15.8 billion, up 39 percent. The company expects 20–25 percent of that to be recognized in the next 12 months. Five-year orders signed so far this year are up 25 percent. Among this quarter’s large contracts was a $258 million AI package and body-camera expansion from a state corrections department.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Management (CEO Rick Smith) | View: demand is strong; three federal orders were only delayed. ; Interest: keep growth around 30 percent, and take the drone lane. ; Worry: the pace of federal purchasing, and supply-chain risk. ; Basis: the shareholder letter says that if the three deployments had been on time, full-year growth would be nearly 500 basis points above the current guide; he called drones “one of the defining technologies of this decade.”

Shareholders and analysts | View: slower growth and a lower guide cannot hold a high valuation. ; Interest: the share price, and certainty about growth. ; Worry: the order target is missed, and quarters swing more. ; Basis: the close on 11-06 was down 18.18 percent; Needham’s target went from $750 to $500; Craig-Hallum cut the rating to “hold.”

Police departments and government customers | View: they want a faster response and tools that save work. ; Interest: efficiency, evidence management, and the budget. ; Worry: a high price, and being tied to one supplier. ; Basis: net revenue retention of 126 percent; in 2023 three U.S. cities filed an antitrust class action saying it had raised body-camera prices (Wikipedia).

Civil-rights and privacy advocates | View: Tasers, AI, and drones are widening what the police can do. ; Interest: civil rights and accountability. ; Worry: surveillance, misuse, and AI getting it wrong. ; Basis: in 2022 Axon proposed drones armed with Tasers for school shootings; its ethics advisory board issued a unanimous objection and nine members resigned; an independent review questioned whether the AI report tool Draft One would “make things up.”

Skydio | View: it gets capital and the largest public-safety channel. ; Interest: scale and valuation. ; Worry: losing its independence. ; Basis: Skydio expects about $1 billion of orders this fiscal year; Axon says Skydio can still develop other industries “freely.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management calls the cut a “delay in timing.” The market reads it as slower growth. The same numbers, two readings.
The company is stocking $100 million of inventory and investing $1.2 billion at the same time. Shareholders worry about cash and returns in the near term.
Drones get the police there faster, and they also make the privacy question sharper. The stronger the product, the larger the ethical dispute.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Axon’s growth depends more and more on large federal orders and on new businesses that are closer to hardware. That revenue arrives on an unsteady timetable and at a lower margin. Whether it can open a new lane and still keep a “software company” margin is the next gate.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The 18.18 percent drop at the close on 11-06 is compiled by the financial press from closing prices. The exchange is the authority.
“Response time cut by as much as 65 percent” and “the drone first in 80 percent of call-outs” are the company’s figures. They have not been checked independently.
Adjusted earnings per share and free cash flow are non-GAAP measures. Analyst expectations differ slightly by data vendor ($1.88 or $1.91).

pieces.title: One meeting, two hosts: COP31 opens, and money and fossil fuels are still the two hurdles
pieces.short: COP31 opens, and money and fossil…
pieces.hook: On 9 November the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) opened in Antalya, on the Mediterranean coast of…
pieces.event: Opened on 11-09 in Antalya, Turkey; scheduled through 11-20

parts: On 9 November the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) opened in Antalya, on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, and runs through 20 November. Nearly 200 countries are taking part, and more than 90,000 people are expected.

Turkey and Australia both bid for this meeting. After the deadlock, a rare split of jobs was fixed last year during COP30 in Brazil. Turkey’s environment minister, Kurum, is president of COP31 and runs the “action agenda”—voluntary initiatives such as electrification, methane, and the circular economy. Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, Bowen, is “president of the negotiations” and chairs the formal talks. Pre-meetings have already been held in the Pacific island countries Fiji and Tuvalu.

paras.lead: A smooth start: the agenda passed quickly
parts: Opening sessions have often argued over the agenda for hours. The opening plenary in Baku in 2024 was delayed a long time for that reason. This time the agenda passed quickly. Bowen said a “presidency-led decision” would be drafted from the first day, rather than left to the last few days.

Already close to 1.5°C] On opening day the World Meteorological Organization reported that from January to September 2026 the global average surface temperature was about 1.47°C above the pre-industrial level, and that this year is likely to be one of the four hottest on record. In October the U.N. Environment Programme warned that going past 1.5°C for a sustained period is already unavoidable, and that current policies point to about 2.8°C of warming this century.

The U.N. Environment Programme estimates that by 2035 developing countries will need about $305 billion a year to adapt to climate change. In 2024 rich countries provided about $30 billion, one tenth of that. Last year in Belém, countries agreed to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035, but they did not write down which year the count starts from.
The first round of the loss-and-damage fund received $2.8 billion in requests and had only $342 million on hand.

paras.lead: A small friction in the agenda
parts: The “climate-finance work programme” set up at COP30 last year was put on the agenda. Carbon Brief reported that the European Union’s representative was “deeply concerned,” worried that last year’s compromise would be opened again. The African Group wanted “tripling adaptation finance” and trade listed as topics of their own. That was refused.

COP28 in Dubai in 2023 agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels,” but last year in Brazil the attempt to write a formal roadmap was blocked by some oil-producing countries. Last week Brazil itself published a voluntary roadmap, asking countries to produce national plans before 2028, with no date for ending coal, oil, and gas.
Turkey is pushing a voluntary target: electricity at 35 percent of global energy use by 2035—without requiring that electricity to be clean.

After Trump announced withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, the U.S. government is not in the negotiations. For the second year running there is no official delegation. A White House official said this summit “refuses to face reality.” About 20 members of Congress went on their own (RFI reported 19). They do not have the State Department’s usual support, and they cannot negotiate for the United States.

This meeting is not chasing a new landmark treaty. It is trying to put promises already made into practice. If it can produce a concrete arrangement on money and a “just transition,” that will be read as a sign that the multilateral machinery can still run. If the argument over money drags to the end, the result may again be a decision that does not bind.

One is to call the “Turkey–Australia split” a rupture. It was agreed last year. Another is to treat “the U.S. government is absent” as “no Americans are there.” Members of Congress are there; they just cannot negotiate. A third is to treat “1.47°C” as already breaching the Paris Agreement. The agreement’s 1.5°C is a multi-decade average, not a single year.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Turkey (the presidency, Kurum) | View: decisions have to land in cities, fields, and factories, and bring household power bills down. ; Interest: the host’s standing, and pushing electrification worldwide. ; Worry: a meeting with no practical result. ; Basis: the opening address (U.N. News); after visiting Tuvalu he said “not a minute, not a day, can be wasted”; the voluntary 35 percent electrification target (RFI).

Australia (president of the negotiations, Bowen) | View: seek the decision that is “the most ambitious and the heaviest on results that consensus will allow.” ; Interest: running the talks, and winning priority items for the Pacific islands. ; Worry: disagreements dragged into the last few days. ; Basis: quoted by U.N. News; in a Guardian interview he was asked whether it is a contradiction for a large fossil-fuel exporter to chair the negotiations.

Developing countries and the African Group | View: the money has to be predictable, and it should be grants, not loans. ; Interest: finance for adaptation and for loss and damage. ; Worry: promises that cannot be cashed, and heavier debt. ; Basis: the African Group chair, Amoah: “the question is not only how much, but on what terms”; Ado of Power Shift Africa: “adaptation is not an option, it is survival.”

The European Union and other developed countries | View: hold last year’s COP30 compromise, and do not reopen the money talks. ; Interest: limiting what they are obliged to pay. ; Worry: a compromise already reached being overturned. ; Basis: Carbon Brief quoted an EU representative as “deeply concerned”; the European Environment Agency reports that the EU can cut emissions about 54 percent by 2030, a little under the legal target of 55 percent.

The United States (the administration, and Democrats in Congress) | View: the administration: this summit “refuses to face reality”; the members of Congress: diplomatic continuity has to be kept. ; Interest: the administration: the fossil-fuel industry; the members: the international standing of the United States. ; Worry: the administration: being bound by climate policy; the members: damage from an empty American chair. ; Basis: the White House official’s remark (the Guardian); Representative Casten: “we have a lot of rebuilding to do.”

Pacific island countries | View: 1.5°C is a line of survival. ; Interest: protecting the ocean, and an easier path to money for sea walls and fresh water. ; Worry: the sea level rising. ; Basis: pre-meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu; a push for stronger ocean protection and easier access to finance (RFI).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Turkey–Australia split sends formal talks and voluntary initiatives down separate tracks. The formal text adds no new obligations, and the voluntary targets do not bind. Both are easier to move, and neither is hard enough.
Developing countries want the money question in every negotiating room. The EU wants to hold last year’s compromise. A small friction on the agenda can grow later.
The U.S. government’s absence removes one source of resistance, and also the largest potential payer. Members of Congress being there sends the signal “we will come back later.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: “At least triple” adaptation finance has no starting year, and the fossil-fuel roadmap has no end date. Without a number and a timetable, a promise is hard to test.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Outlets do not agree how many members of Congress went (19, or about 20).
The meeting has only just opened. What each side says now is an opening position. The final text may look very different.
“1.47°C” is the figure for January to September. The full-year result waits on the World Meteorological Organization’s formal report.
